unit.title: Your Pickleball Path
unit.summary: Find your journey: are you a player, a fan, or both? Explore what each path means.

lessons.title: Choose your path
lessons.objective: Understand the four pickleball journeys and find yours.

payload.prompt: She says she plays three nights a week and watches the pros on weekends. Where do you start?

situation.narrative: She is describing her pickleball life and you are working out which path to learn first.

options.label: Ask which part she is most excited to talk about
options.consequence: She answers right away, and you know which path to learn first. She also loves that you asked.
considerations: Her excitement tells you where to start

options.label: Learn the pro side first because it is easier to look up
options.consequence: You will have plenty to say about the pros, but you may miss the part of pickleball that fills most of her week.
considerations: Pro info is easy to find
Her own play may matter more to her
It is a fine second step

options.label: Assume she only cares about her own games
options.consequence: You just skipped half of what she told you, and it may show when she mentions a pro match.
considerations: She said she watches the pros
You might miss an easy bonding topic

payload.expertNote: Most people sit somewhere between playing and watching. Ask what she is most excited about, and follow that path first.

payload.prompt: Match each pickleball path to what she'd talk about.

pairs.definition: Local open play, paddle stack, DUPR ratings, court community.
Individual pro events, world rankings, player rivalries.
Team franchises, rosters, standings, DreamBreaker tiebreaks.
Amateur-pro tournaments, regional events, division brackets.

distractorDefinitions: A fitness class at the gym

explanation.summary: Four paths, each with its own culture and focus: local play, individual pros, team fandom and the amateur circuit.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rec is local play. PPA is individual pros. MLP is teams. APP is the amateur circuit.

payload.prompt: Choosing a path means you stop learning the core game. True?

choices.label: No, every path shares the core game
Yes, you only learn your path

explanation.correct: Right. The kitchen, the serve and the scoring are the same everywhere. Your path just changes the examples and the live news you see.
explanation.incorrect: The core game is shared across every path. Your path changes the examples and the context, not the rules.
explanation.sayThisLine: Same game underneath. The path just changes what we talk about.

payload.prompt: Which tour uses a team-based league format?

options.text: PPA Tour (individual brackets)
MLP (team franchises, rosters)
APP Tour (amateur-pro mix)
All of them

explanation.correct: MLP is Major League Pickleball: franchises, teams and rosters.
explanation.incorrect: MLP is the team league. The PPA and APP are built around individual brackets.
explanation.sayThisLine: MLP is teams. PPA is individuals. APP is the amateur circuit.

payload.prompt: Complete the path statement.
payload.template: The PPA features {{format1}} players, while {{tour2}} features {{format2}} competition.

explanation.correct: The PPA is built on individual players and partners in brackets. MLP is built on franchises and teams.
explanation.incorrect: The two tours differ on structure: individual brackets for the PPA, team franchises for MLP.
explanation.sayThisLine: PPA is individual. MLP is team-based.

lessons.title: Playing locally
lessons.objective: Learn open play, ratings and the local court community.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I need to get my paddle in the stack before it fills up.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Paddles are lined up to show who plays next; she wants her spot in the line.
She's organizing all the paddles in a neat pile.
She's buying more paddles at the store.
She's stacking paddles as a prank.

payload.translation: In open play, paddles line up to show who is waiting for the next game. She wants her place in line.

followUps.line: So the paddles show who's up next?
followUps.why: Checks your understanding and lets her explain her courts' system.

followUps.line: At your courts, do winners stay on or does everybody rotate?
followUps.why: Courts differ, so asking shows curiosity instead of assuming.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Many courts let winners stay on, but others rotate everyone, so ask how hers works.

payload.prompt: A 4.0 is about the level of a touring pro. True?

explanation.correct: Right. A 4.0 is a strong, experienced player, but touring pros sit far above that on the scale.
explanation.incorrect: The scale runs from about 2.5 to 5.0 and beyond. A 4.0 is strong and experienced, while pros are well above it.
explanation.sayThisLine: 4.0 is a strong player. The pros are in a different league.

payload.prompt: Her self-rating is 3.5 but her DUPR is 3.7. How do you read that?

situation.narrative: She shows you two numbers and asks what you make of the gap.

options.label: DUPR follows her results, so she may be playing a bit above 3.5
options.consequence: That is a fair read. DUPR comes from match results, so it is a useful hint, though not a perfect one.

options.label: Ask which number she trusts more and why
options.consequence: A nice conversation starter, but you did not show what you have learned about what DUPR is.
considerations: Skips the chance to share what you know

options.label: Say her own number is better because she chose it
options.consequence: A self-rating is just her opinion, and people are often off in either direction. It is usually less informative than results.

payload.expertNote: DUPR (Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating) is built from recorded match results, which makes it a useful guide. It is still only a guide.

payload.prompt: Match rec-play terms to their meanings.

pairs.definition: Drop-in games at a court where paddles line up and players rotate in.
A number (3.0, 3.5, 4.0, etc.) describing your playing level.
Habits like calling lines fairly, warming up with courtesy and respecting others.

explanation.summary: Open play is casual drop-in pickleball, ratings describe skill, and etiquette keeps it friendly.
explanation.sayThisLine: Open play is drop-in. A rating is your level. Etiquette is respect.

payload.title: Her week at the courts
payload.setting: Sam is walking you through her usual week of pickleball.

exchanges.theirMessage: Monday is ladies' night, Wednesday is league, and Saturday morning is open play. That's basically my week.

replies.text: That's a full week! Which night is your favorite?
replies.theirResponse: Saturday open play. Everyone knows everyone and there's always a good game.
replies.coachNote: You noticed the rhythm of her week and asked what she loves.

replies.text: Wow, that's a lot of pickleball.
replies.coachNote: Friendly, but it does not ask her anything.

replies.text: Do you have a life outside pickleball?
replies.theirResponse: This is my life. Wow, okay.
replies.coachNote: Playful is fine, but never tease the thing she loves.

exchanges.theirMessage: League is tough, though. I'm the weakest player on my team.

replies.text: What part of your game do you want to work on?
replies.theirResponse: Honestly my drop. If I fix that, I'll feel way better about it.
replies.coachNote: You invited her to share a goal instead of giving advice.

replies.theirResponse: Thanks, that's sweet, but you haven't seen me play.
replies.coachNote: Kind, but it skips what she actually said.

replies.theirResponse: I don't want to quit. I want to get better.
replies.coachNote: Do not solve it by removing the thing she loves.

payload.closingNote: A rec week has a rhythm: open play, league nights, ladies' night. Asking which one she loves most is a great opener.

payload.prompt: Complete the open play statement.
payload.template: In open play, your {{item1}} goes in the stack, and you {{action1}} until it's your turn.

explanation.correct: The paddle stack is the queue. You put your paddle in line and wait for your turn.
explanation.incorrect: Open play is self-organized, and the paddles in line show who is next. Your shoes stay on you.
explanation.sayThisLine: Stack your paddle, wait your turn, cheer on the courts.

lessons.title: Her level, her struggle
lessons.objective: Recognise what each level usually struggles with.

payload.prompt: Match each level to a common focus.

pairs.definition: Keeping the ball in play and learning the kitchen and scoring.
A reliable third-shot drop and fewer unforced errors.
Resets, hand speed and choosing the right moment to speed up.

distractorDefinitions: Learning which brand of paddle to buy
Choosing a team in the MLP draft

explanation.summary: As players improve, the struggle moves from keeping the ball in play to building the third-shot drop to choosing smart moments to attack. These are common themes, not a rulebook.
explanation.sayThisLine: At 3.5 it's usually the drop. At 4.0 it's more about when to speed up.

payload.prompt: What are many 3.5 players working on?

options.text: A reliable third-shot drop and fewer unforced errors.
Learning which side to serve from.
Coaching touring pros.
Switching to singles only.

explanation.correct: At 3.5 the basics are in place, so the big gains come from consistent drops and cutting errors.
explanation.incorrect: Serving sides are a beginner topic, and 3.5 players are not coaching pros. The common focus is a steadier third shot and fewer errors.
explanation.sayThisLine: At 3.5 everyone seems to be working on their drop.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I'm a 3.5 and my dinks keep floating up. It's so annoying.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: That sounds frustrating. Are they popping up, or going into the net?
Just hit them harder.
That's 3.5 for you. Deal with it.
You should stop dinking altogether.

payload.translation: She is struggling with soft shots that pop up high enough for opponents to attack.

followUps.line: Is it happening more when they hit it fast or slow?
followUps.why: A specific follow-up shows you listened, without pretending to coach.

followUps.line: What does your group say helps?
followUps.why: Invites her to share what she is already trying.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You are not her coach. Ask about the problem and let her do the diagnosing.

payload.prompt: Every 3.5 player struggles with the exact same things. True?

choices.label: No, levels only hint at common themes
Yes, each level has identical problems

explanation.correct: Right. Levels show common themes, but every player has her own weak spots, which is why asking beats assuming.
explanation.incorrect: A level is a rough guide. Two 3.5 players can have very different strengths, so ask about hers.
explanation.sayThisLine: What's the thing you're fighting with at your level?

payload.prompt: Complete the level statement.
payload.template: At {{level}}, many players are working on a reliable {{skill}}.

explanation.correct: The third-shot drop is a classic 3.5 project because it lets a team move up to the kitchen line.
explanation.incorrect: Serves are underhand in pickleball, so an overhand serve is not a skill at any level. The classic 3.5 project is the third-shot drop.
explanation.sayThisLine: A lot of 3.5s are chasing a consistent drop.

lessons.title: PPA Tour watching
lessons.objective: Follow the PPA Tour, events and world rankings.

payload.prompt: What defines the PPA Tour?

options.text: Individual pro players competing in brackets and slams
Team franchises playing scheduled matches
A league of amateur tournaments
Local court rankings

explanation.correct: The PPA is an individual pro circuit built around events, brackets and world rankings.
explanation.incorrect: The PPA is about pros and their partners competing against each other in tournaments, not franchises or local ladders.
explanation.sayThisLine: PPA Tour means individual pros and bracket tournaments.

payload.prompt: Put these PPA event stages in order.

explanation.sayThisLine: Draw, rounds, semis, final, champion. Standard tournament flow.
explanation.correct: Events flow from the bracket through the rounds to a champion, with points awarded at the end.
explanation.incorrect: Pro events follow a bracket: the draw comes first, then the rounds narrow the field through semis and the final.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: She just won a slam, so her ranking should jump.

payload.question: What does a slam mean?

options.text: A major pro event with the most ranking points
A really loud hit at the net
A losing streak
A local tournament

payload.translation: A slam is a prestige event with big point rewards.

followUps.line: So winning a slam moves her up the rankings fast?
followUps.why: Checks your understanding and invites her to fill in details.

followUps.line: Which slam is the one everyone wants?
followUps.why: Shows interest without claiming knowledge of any one event.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Slams are the major tournaments, worth the most points. Do not guess which events count as slams; ask.

payload.prompt: PPA events have separate men's, women's and mixed brackets. True?

choices.label: Yes, each has its own bracket
No, everyone is in one bracket

explanation.correct: Yes. Events run separate brackets, including men's, women's and mixed doubles, so there are several champions per event.
explanation.incorrect: Pro events split into brackets such as men's, women's and mixed doubles, which is why one event can crown several champions.
explanation.sayThisLine: Which bracket are you watching this weekend?

payload.prompt: Match PPA terms to their meanings.

pairs.definition: The tournament structure showing seeding and who plays whom.
Ranking players by skill to give top players easier early matches.
A major tournament with the highest ranking-point rewards.

explanation.summary: The bracket organizes the event, seeding ranks players, and slams award the most points.
explanation.sayThisLine: Bracket is the structure. Seed is the rank. Slam is the major.

lessons.title: MLP team fandom
lessons.objective: Follow MLP franchises, rosters and the DreamBreaker.

payload.prompt: What does MLP stand for and how is it different from PPA?

options.text: Major League Pickleball; it's team-based, not individual
Minor League Pickleball; it's for amateurs
Multi-Level Pickleball; it has mixed divisions
It's the same as PPA

explanation.correct: MLP is Major League Pickleball, a team league. The PPA is an individual pro circuit.
explanation.incorrect: MLP features franchises and team rosters. The PPA is built on individual tournaments.
explanation.sayThisLine: MLP is teams. PPA is individuals. Same sport, different structure.

payload.prompt: Order an MLP team's season from start to finish.

items.text: Standings decide who reaches the playoffs

explanation.sayThisLine: Regular season, standings, playoffs, finals. That's a team's whole story.
explanation.correct: A team's season builds through regular-season wins, the standings set the playoff field, and the playoffs lead to the final.
explanation.incorrect: The season runs in order: regular-season wins build the standings, the standings set the playoff field, and the playoffs lead to the finals.

payload.prompt: A DreamBreaker tiebreaker is played to 11 points. True?

choices.label: No, it's played to 21 with rally scoring
Yes, it's to 11 like normal games

explanation.correct: The DreamBreaker is rally scoring to 21, not the standard 11.
explanation.incorrect: The DreamBreaker is a special tiebreak: rally scoring, played to 21.
explanation.sayThisLine: The DreamBreaker is rally scoring to 21.

payload.prompt: Her team sits one spot outside the playoff line. What does that mean?

situation.narrative: She is checking an imaginary table late in the season, and it is tense.

facts.label: Her team
facts.value: One spot outside the last playoff place

facts.label: Stakes
facts.value: Miss the line and the season ends

options.label: They are on the bubble and every remaining win matters
options.consequence: Right. She is on the edge of the playoff picture, so each match counts and the tension is real.
considerations: The cut line decides who continues
Two events left means little room

options.label: They are locked into the playoffs already
options.consequence: Not yet. They are outside the line, so they still have to climb past a team ahead of them.
considerations: Outside the line means not in yet
Saying they are in would sting

payload.expertNote: Standings turn into drama late in the season. Ask how her team is doing and where the cut line is.

payload.title: Roster news
payload.setting: Sam texts you about a roster move on her MLP team.

exchanges.theirMessage: My team just added a new mixed-doubles player. I'm cautiously optimistic.

replies.text: Cautiously? What would make you fully optimistic?
replies.theirResponse: If they click with our lineup early. Chemistry matters so much.
replies.coachNote: You picked up her word and asked about it.
Warm, but make it a question about how she feels.

replies.text: Teams do that all the time. Relax.
replies.theirResponse: Wow, okay. I'm allowed to care.

exchanges.theirMessage: If we make the playoffs I'm going to scream.

replies.text: Where are they in the standings right now?
replies.theirResponse: Right on the bubble. Which is why I'm stressing.
replies.coachNote: A question about her team shows you care.
Kind, but a question would land better.

replies.theirResponse: Yes. Really. It's a big deal to me.
replies.coachNote: Do not shrink what she loves.

payload.closingNote: Team fandom runs on rosters, standings and playoff hopes. Ask about her team and let her do the talking.

payload.prompt: Match MLP terms to their meanings.

pairs.definition: A team in the Major League Pickleball league.
Four games between two franchises; if 2-2, goes to DreamBreaker.
A rally-scoring tiebreak to 21 when a match is tied 2-2.

explanation.summary: A franchise is a team, a match is four games between two franchises, and the DreamBreaker settles a 2-2 tie.
explanation.sayThisLine: Franchise is the team. Match is four games. DreamBreaker is the tiebreak.

lessons.title: The amateur circuit
lessons.objective: Follow APP events, tournament divisions and amateur-pro play.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I'm thinking about my first APP tournament next month.

payload.question: What is an APP tournament?

options.text: An Association of Pickleball Players event mixing amateurs and pros
A mobile app for scheduling games
A professional-only bracket
A practice round before PPA

payload.translation: APP stands for Association of Pickleball Players. Its events include both amateur and pro brackets.

followUps.line: Which division are you thinking of entering?
followUps.why: A practical question shows you understand divisions.

followUps.line: Is it your first tournament ever?
followUps.why: Shows interest in her experience instead of quizzing her.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: APP is the amateur circuit that also includes pro brackets. Ask about her plan, not the rules.

payload.prompt: How are tournament divisions commonly split?

options.text: By skill level and often by age group
By paddle brand
By how long a player has played
By the player's home city only

explanation.correct: Divisions group similar players, usually by skill level such as 3.5 or 4.0, and often by age and event type too, so matches are fair.
explanation.incorrect: Divisions are about fairness: skill level and age group, plus event types like men's, women's or mixed. Brand and home city are not used.
explanation.sayThisLine: Divisions group people so matches are fair. Which one are you in?

payload.prompt: Her DUPR is 3.8 and she is unsure which division to enter. What do you say?

situation.narrative: She is signing up for her first tournament and asks what you think.

facts.label: Experience
facts.value: Open play twice a week for two years

options.label: Suggest she check the event's rating rules and enter honestly
options.consequence: Good call. Events have their own entry rules, and an honest division is fairer to everyone, including her.

options.label: Admit you do not know divisions well and ask how she usually decides
options.consequence: Honest and curious, though you could have pointed her to the event's rules.

options.label: Tell her to enter the lower division so she can win easily
options.consequence: That is sandbagging. Entering below her level to win is unfair to the other players, and it is the kind of thing people complain about.
considerations: Entering below your level is sandbagging
It spoils the day for others
Wins earned unfairly do not feel good

payload.expertNote: Rating rules differ by event. The honest move is to check them, enter where she genuinely fits, and focus on enjoying the day.

payload.prompt: The APP Tour is professional-only. True?

choices.label: No, it mixes amateur and pro players

explanation.correct: The APP is the Association of Pickleball Players circuit, and its events include both amateur and pro brackets.
explanation.incorrect: The APP Tour is amateur-friendly and includes pro-amateur brackets, so it is not professional-only.
explanation.sayThisLine: The APP is where amateurs and pros share the stage.

payload.prompt: Match amateur circuit terms to their meanings.

pairs.definition: Association of Pickleball Players; amateur and pro brackets.
A skill-level bracket in a tournament (3.5, 4.0, etc.).
The structure pairing you with opponents at your skill level.

explanation.summary: The APP is the amateur circuit. Divisions and brackets organize fair play.
explanation.sayThisLine: APP is the amateur path. A division is your level. A bracket is the match structure.

lessons.title: Her favorite player
lessons.objective: Learn how to talk about her favorite pro without faking it.

payload.prompt: Which detail helps you talk about her favorite pro?

options.text: Their playing style and signature shot.
Their shoe size.
How much a paddle contract is worth.
Their follower count.

explanation.correct: Style and signature shot tell you what she enjoys watching, and they give you natural things to ask about.
explanation.incorrect: Shoe size, contracts and follower counts do not show what she loves about the game. A style and a signature shot do.
explanation.sayThisLine: What is it about how she plays that you love?

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: She's my favorite because of her hands game.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Quick, sharp volleys and exchanges at the kitchen line.
She catches the ball by hand between points.
She has unusually big hands.
She claps a lot after winning points.

payload.translation: A great hands game means quick, accurate volleys in the fast exchanges at the net.

followUps.line: Do you like watching her at the kitchen line?
followUps.why: Connects her phrase to what you have learned.

followUps.line: Is there a point where her hands really won it?
followUps.why: Invites a story instead of pretending to know the highlight.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to know the player. Ask what she sees in the style.

payload.prompt: She gushes about a pro you have never heard of. Your move?

situation.narrative: She is lit up describing her favorite player, and you do not recognize the name.

options.label: Say you don't know them yet and ask what she loves about how they play
options.consequence: She grins and gives you a whole scouting report. Being honest made her more excited, not less.
considerations: She gets to be the expert
You learn a style and a shot

options.label: Nod along and look them up afterwards
options.consequence: You will catch up, but she may realize you were nodding along without understanding.

options.label: Pretend you know them and mention a match
options.consequence: She asks which match, and now you are caught. Faking expertise is the quickest way to lose trust.

payload.expertNote: Never fake it. Admitting you do not know a player yet is charming, and it invites her to teach you.

payload.prompt: Order a good way to ask about her favorite pro.

items.text: Ask who her favorite pro is
Ask what she loves about how they play
Listen for a shot or style word she uses
Ask a follow-up about that word

explanation.sayThisLine: Who's your favorite? What do you love about them? Tell me more about that.
explanation.correct: Start with who, move to why, listen for a detail she mentions, then follow up on it.
explanation.incorrect: Ask who first, then why, then pick up a detail she gives you and follow up. That order keeps the conversation about her.

lessons.title: Her home court
lessons.objective: Understand her local scene: courts, regulars and hours.

payload.prompt: What is a good way to learn about her home court scene?

options.text: Ask which times are busiest and who the regulars are.
Guess when it's quiet and show up.
Tell her what you think is wrong with her courts.
Skip asking and assume it's like every other court.

explanation.correct: Asking about busy times and regulars shows interest, and it gives you the real picture from someone who plays there.
explanation.incorrect: Every court has its own rhythm, so guessing or assuming misses it. Asking her is friendlier and more accurate.
explanation.sayThisLine: When's the best time to come? Who should I meet first?

payload.prompt: She says her courts are packed on weekends and you want to join. Your move?

situation.narrative: She mentions how busy her courts get, and you would love to come along.

facts.label: You
facts.value: New, and unsure how they rotate

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: Join without being in the way

options.label: Ask when it's friendliest for newcomers and how they rotate
options.consequence: She gives you a good time to come and explains how the stack works. You look considerate.

options.label: Ask her to save a court for you at peak time
options.consequence: She may try, but saving courts is often frowned on at busy places, and it puts her in an awkward spot.
considerations: Courts are usually first come, first served

options.label: Show up at peak time and expect a game
options.consequence: You may wait a long time, and you will not know the rotation. A quieter time would go better.
considerations: Quieter times are kinder to newcomers

payload.expertNote: Ask about the newcomer-friendly times and how her courts rotate. Every scene has its own rhythm.

payload.prompt: Every local court uses the same hours and rotation rules. True?

choices.label: No, every court has its own setup

explanation.correct: Right. Hours, reservations and rotation are set locally, so every court works a little differently.
explanation.incorrect: Local courts differ on hours, reservations and how players rotate. That is why asking a regular is the smartest first step.
explanation.sayThisLine: How does it work at your courts?

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Our courts are always packed on weekends, so we go early.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Smart. How early do people start showing up?
Why don't they build more courts?
Just play somewhere else.
That's a waste of time.

payload.translation: Popular courts fill up, so regulars plan around it by arriving early.

followUps.line: Is there a regular crowd, or does everyone rotate in?
What's the vibe like when it's that busy?
followUps.why: Invites a story about her local scene.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need solutions. Show interest in how her scene works.
